setting: UK; steel-framed buildings
sample_and_measure: 23 designs; 10,130 valid beams and 1,837 columns
finding: Reported mean beam utilisation 0.40 (unweighted) and 0.54 (mass-weighted); mean column utilisation 0.49
comparison_limit: Selected projects; one material; appraisal and weighting affect comparison
reference: Moynihan, M. C., and Allwood, J. M. (2014). Utilization of structural steel in buildings. Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 470(2168), 20140170.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary open text checked for retained counts and unweighted versus mass-weighted means.
dataset_overlap_note: Selected designs from three consultancies; no pooled comparison is made.

setting: UK; steel-frame floor plates
sample_and_measure: 30 cases: 27 real and 3 models; governing utilisation
finding: 36% estimated unused steel mass under appraisal assumptions
comparison_limit: Floor plates only; mass estimate is not measured removable material
reference: Dunant, C. F., Drewniok, M. P., Eleftheriadis, S., Cullen, J. M., and Allwood, J. M. (2018). Regularity and optimisation practice in steel structural frames in real design cases. Resources, Conservation and Recycling, 134, 294–302.
evidence_access_and_verification: Comparator retained in the paper’s Table 1; governing checks and conditional unused-mass appraisal retained.
dataset_overlap_note: Dunant et al. (2021) reuses 19 designs from this floor-plate database; no separate entry is added.

setting: Kuwait; reinforced-concrete villas
sample_and_measure: Six villas; existing reinforcement compared with ACI redesign at unchanged concrete dimensions
finding: Redesign identified excess reinforcement in the existing designs
comparison_limit: Small selected sample; quantity comparison rather than recorded governing utilisation; primary abstract does not quantify the excess
reference: Sadek, A. W., Al-Fadala, S., and Al-Mutairi, N. (2006). Improving the design of residential buildings in Kuwait. Emirates Journal for Engineering Research, 11(2), 59–65.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary abstract confirms six villas and overdesign. The numerical excess figures quoted by Alnuaimi were not independently verified in the primary full text and are excluded.
dataset_overlap_note: Predecessor of the Oman redesign study; separate country/sample, not a replicated utilisation distribution.

setting: Oman; reinforced-concrete villas
sample_and_measure: 31 villas; provided versus redesigned reinforcement
finding: 48.5% average excess relative to redesign requirement
comparison_limit: Quantity comparison rather than governing utilisation; minor overall cost effect
reference: Alnuaimi, A. S., Al Mohsin, M., Hago, A., and El Gamal, S. (2015). Overdesign of villa structures in Oman. The Journal of Engineering Research, 12(2), 68–76.
evidence_access_and_verification: Publisher abstract checked for 31 villas, 48.5% reinforcement excess, and minor overall cost effect. Publisher citation supplies pages 68–76.
dataset_overlap_note: Distinct from Sadek et al. (2006); reinforcement redesign outcome.

setting: Cambridge study; in-situ concrete frames; project locations not stated
sample_and_measure: Sample RC projects; beam utilisation and slab-thickness appraisal; counts not reported in abstract
finding: Mean beam utilisation about 0.70; slabs about 0.85 utilised by thickness, with lower reinforcement utilisation
comparison_limit: Abstract-level evidence; sample size and detailed checks unavailable; slab thickness is a different utilisation measure
reference: Forster, P. (2016, October). Quantifying the opportunity to reduce material use in insitu reinforced concrete frames. Construction Engineering Masters dissertation abstract, University of Cambridge.
evidence_access_and_verification: One-page primary abstract only. Signature reads Peter Forster, October 2016. Sample/member counts and full appraisal methods are unavailable; none are inferred.
dataset_overlap_note: Beam, slab-thickness and reinforcement utilisation are distinct measures within the same dissertation.

setting: UK non-seismic context; existing concrete columns
sample_and_measure: Appraisal of overdesign factors; typical 1960s flats
finding: 32% minimum and 85% likely reserve under stated assumptions
comparison_limit: Conditional reserve estimates; not a routine-calculation distribution
reference: Mei, X., Hawkins, W., Darby, A., and Ibell, T. (2024). Realising the reserve capacity in existing reinforced concrete columns. Structures, 63, 106360.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary university publication record/abstract checked for conditional minimum 32% and likely 85% reserve.
dataset_overlap_note: Existing-building appraisal; no observed routine-design sample is inferred.

setting: UK Eurocode context; non-composite steel beams
sample_and_measure: Catalogue-based redesign with fixed layout
finding: 26.5% mass savings in original-constraint scenario
comparison_limit: Conditional optimisation outcome, rather than routine-practice prevalence
reference: Drewniok, M. P., Campbell, J., and Orr, J. (2020). The Lightest Beam Method – A methodology to find ultimate steel savings and reduce embodied carbon in steel framed buildings. Structures, 27, 687–701.
evidence_access_and_verification: Comparator retained in the paper’s Table 1; retain the original-constraint scenario for the 26.5% mass saving.
dataset_overlap_note: Conditional catalogue redesign; no additional observed practice population.

setting: UK code context; steel office frames
sample_and_measure: 11,252 hypothetical configurations; 11 scenarios
finding: Reserve and extension potential vary with design and appraisal
comparison_limit: Generated cases do not establish observed utilisation frequencies
reference: Gillott, C., Davison, B., and Densley Tingley, D. (2025). Reserve capacity and vertical extension potential in steel-frame buildings. Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers – Structures and Buildings, 178(3), 235–247.
evidence_access_and_verification: Comparator retained in the paper’s Table 1; 11,252 generated configurations and 11 scenarios retained.
dataset_overlap_note: Hypothetical cases must not be combined with counts of observed projects or members.

setting: Australia, South East Queensland; concrete office slabs
sample_and_measure: One 10-storey office; reinforced and post-tensioned slab alternatives; material quantities
finding: Post-tensioned alternative used 36.9% less concrete volume and 43.4% less steel mass
comparison_limit: Single design comparison of alternative slab systems; savings are conditional on the study design, rather than observed reserve
reference: Miller, D., Doh, J.-H., Guan, H., Mulvey, M., Fragomeni, S., McCarthy, T., and Peters, T. (2013). Environmental impact assessment of post tensioned and reinforced concrete slab construction. In From Materials to Structures: Advancement through Innovation. CRC Press.
evidence_access_and_verification: Chapter text checked in the source review for the 10-storey reference office and 36.9% concrete/43.4% steel differences. Publication year and the seven-author list were reconciled against the Griffith University repository record on 28 October 2026; ACMSM 2012 is the conference name.
dataset_overlap_note: Two slab-system alternatives for one reference office, not two independent buildings.

setting: Australia, Sydney reference location; timber versus concrete or steel
sample_and_measure: Four building types: office, apartment, aged care and industrial shed; structural cost plans
finding: Timber structural costs lower by 12.4%, 2.2%, 13.9% and 9.4%, respectively
comparison_limit: Industry costing of alternative systems at a specified location and date; measures cost, rather than utilisation or removable material
reference: Dunn, A. (2015, January). Final report for commercial building costing case studies – Traditional design versus timber project. Forest and Wood Products Australia, project PNA308-1213.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary report checked for Andrew Dunn, January 2015, project identifier and the four structural-cost comparisons.
dataset_overlap_note: Four costed archetypes at a reference location/date; alternative systems are paired comparisons.

setting: Australia-based study; parametric tall-building systems
sample_and_measure: 80 structural systems; finite-element design and hybrid life-cycle inventory analysis
finding: Changing structural design methods changed embodied greenhouse-gas emissions by up to 22%
comparison_limit: Modelled systems; sensitivity to design and appraisal assumptions, rather than observed member-utilisation frequencies
reference: Helal, J., Stephan, A., and Crawford, R. H. (2020). The influence of structural design methods on the embodied greenhouse gas emissions of structural systems for tall buildings. Structures, 24, 650–665.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary abstract/paper text checked for 80 systems and up to 22% sensitivity to design method.
dataset_overlap_note: The separate IOP paper on life-cycle inventory methods is not another utilisation dataset.

setting: UK research; thin-shell concrete floors versus flat slabs
sample_and_measure: Design comparisons across 6–18 m spans; equivalent structural performance
finding: Thin-shell floors reduced embodied carbon by 53–58% and self-weight by 43–53%
comparison_limit: Conditional floor-system redesign; requires a different structural form and construction method; no prevalence estimate
reference: Hawkins, W., Orr, J., Ibell, T., and Shepherd, P. (2020). A design methodology to reduce the embodied carbon of concrete buildings using thin-shell floors. Engineering Structures, 110195.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary Cambridge repository abstract checked for spans, carbon and self-weight comparisons.
dataset_overlap_note: Floor-form strategy evidence; related thin-shell scenarios also occur in Jayasinghe et al. (2022).

setting: UK office-floor scenarios; concrete floor systems
sample_and_measure: Parametric spans and floor types; cradle-to-gate embodied carbon versus conventional flat slabs
finding: Savings up to 12% from depth/grade, 23% from post-tensioning, 36% from alternative conventional slabs and 65% from thin shells
comparison_limit: Strategy-specific scenario maxima; percentages cannot be added or read as observed unused capacity
reference: Jayasinghe, A., Orr, J., Hawkins, W., Ibell, T., and Boshoff, W. P. (2022). Comparing different strategies of minimising embodied carbon in concrete floors. Journal of Cleaner Production, 131177.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary abstract/results text checked for strategy-specific maxima. The maxima are not additive.
dataset_overlap_note: Overlapping strategy family with thin-shell research; entries are publications, not independent pooled observations.

setting: Australia; mid-rise mass-timber and post-tensioned concrete buildings
sample_and_measure: Two reference buildings; Monte Carlo uncertainty in life-cycle embodied carbon
finding: Timber 196–590 kgCO2e/m² (mean 417); concrete 307–618 (mean 465); mean difference 48 kgCO2e/m²
comparison_limit: Whole-building carbon under inventory and life-cycle assumptions; overlapping ranges; no member reserve or routine-practice distribution
reference: Robati, M., and Oldfield, P. (2022). The embodied carbon of mass timber and concrete buildings in Australia: An uncertainty analysis. Building and Environment, 214, 108944.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary repository abstract checked in the expanded-table review for two reference buildings, ranges and means; uncertainty scope retained.
dataset_overlap_note: Monte Carlo outcomes from two reference buildings; ranges are not a sample of observed member reserve.

setting: Australia-based study; lightweight residential frame
sample_and_measure: One archetype; timber, steel and timber–steel composite frame options assessed using finite-element models
finding: Embodied carbon 35.56% lower for timber and 8.12% lower for timber–steel composite than for steel
comparison_limit: Single-archetype material and system comparison; embodied-carbon differences are not governing utilisation ratios
reference: Huang, B., Xing, K., and Rameezdeen, R. (2023). Exploring embodied carbon comparison in lightweight building structure frames: A case study. Sustainability, 15(20), 15167.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary article text checked for 35.56% timber and 8.12% hybrid reductions relative to steel.
dataset_overlap_note: Three frame options for one archetype, not three independent practice samples.

setting: US design and policy context; steel and concrete buildings
sample_and_measure: Parametric building configurations; modelled embodied-carbon savings from policy and design strategies
finding: Buy Clean savings about 9% (steel) and 16% (concrete); span reduction or shape-optimised floors yielded up to about 70% and 79%
comparison_limit: Modelled, strategy-dependent savings against specified baselines; no observed utilisation sample or directly removable-material estimate
reference: Feickert, K., and Mueller, C. T. (2025). Policy and design levers for minimizing embodied carbon in United States buildings: A quantitative comparison of current and proposed strategies. Building and Environment, 270, 112485.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary publisher abstract checked for approximate policy and design savings; scenario/baseline dependence retained.
dataset_overlap_note: Parametric policy/design comparisons; generated alternatives are not observed utilisation frequencies.

setting: US and Canada; steel and reinforced concrete
sample_and_measure: 226 designed systems from one firm; quantities and carbon
finding: Component-level evidence on material and emissions
comparison_limit: Does not measure governing utilisation or variation across firms
reference: Fang, D., Kenny, P., and Mueller, C. (2026). Material efficiency as a key opportunity to reduce embodied carbon in structural systems: Data insights from 226 fully designed projects. Journal of Structural Engineering, 152(2), 04025275.
evidence_access_and_verification: Comparator retained in the paper’s Table 1; source metadata taken from the reference record; quantities/carbon measure distinguished from D/C.
dataset_overlap_note: One-firm programme overlaps the earlier Thornton Tomasetti tracking programme. Possible overlap with other project databases is not resolved; counts are not summed.

setting: Industry building survey; country split not reported
sample_and_measure: 200 recently completed buildings; structural material mass and cradle-to-gate embodied CO2 per floor area
finding: Structural quantities 200–1,800 kg/m²; embodied CO2 150–600 kgCO2e/m²
comparison_limit: Multi-firm quantity and carbon evidence; no member demand-to-capacity ratios; country coverage cannot be inferred from affiliations
reference: De Wolf, C., Yang, F., Cox, D., Charlson, A., Hattan, A. S., and Ochsendorf, J. (2016). Material quantities and embodied carbon dioxide in structures. Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers – Engineering Sustainability, 169(4), 150–161.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary Crossref abstract checked for 200 buildings and quantity/carbon ranges. Country distribution is not reported.
dataset_overlap_note: Contributing industry datasets may recur in later compilations, including CLF; no pooling is justified.

study: Simonen et al. (2017), CLF benchmark study
setting: Worldwide compilation; structure, foundation and enclosure
sample_and_measure: Over 1,000 buildings; compiled initial embodied-carbon intensities (LCA stage A)
finding: Initial embodied carbon typically below 1,000 kgCO2e/m²; 200–500 kgCO2e/m² covered 50% of commercial offices
comparison_limit: Non-representative compilation with unaligned LCA methods and possible overlap with contributing datasets; carbon, rather than utilisation
reference: Simonen, K., Rodriguez, B., McDade, E., and Strain, L. (2017). Embodied carbon benchmark study: LCA for low carbon construction. Carbon Leadership Forum, University of Washington.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary report checked in the expanded-table review for broad initial-carbon ranges and non-representativeness. Report authors follow its suggested citation, distinguished from the associated database authors.
dataset_overlap_note: Includes contributed datasets, including MIT deQo/Thornton Tomasetti. Methods and scopes are unaligned and overlap is possible.

study: Fang et al. (2024), SE 2050 executive summary
setting: Primarily US; mixed building structural systems
sample_and_measure: 522 submissions; filtered upfront-carbon n = 241 and A-to-C n = 100; structural GWP intensity
finding: 350 kgCO2e/m² proposed as an 80th-percentile upper limit for upfront structural GWP intensity, excluding biogenic carbon
comparison_limit: Submitted-project carbon benchmark; subsets must be distinguished; spread limits precise system-specific benchmarks; no governing utilisation
reference: Fang, D., Chafart, M., Torres, M., and Broyles, J. (2024). Executive summary of the SE 2050 Commitment Program 2023 Data Analysis and Findings Report. Edited by L. Wingo, Z. Chabot, and E. Borchers. SE 2050.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary executive summary read for 522 submissions, upfront subset 241, A-to-C subset 100 and proposed 350 kgCO2e/m² upper limit; biogenic carbon excluded.
dataset_overlap_note: Subsets are not independent additional projects. Firm contributions may overlap other structural-carbon programmes; no combined total is reported.

study: Benke et al. (2024), California Carbon Report
setting: US, California; structure and enclosure
sample_and_measure: 30 new buildings from CLF WBLCA Benchmark Study v2; 60-year carbon assessment
finding: Median embodied-carbon intensity of structure and enclosure 390 kgCO2e/m²
comparison_limit: Regional, scope-limited LCA sample from the same CLF v2 programme; do not sum with the 292-project dataset; no utilisation ratios
reference: Benke, B., Roberts, M., Shen, Y., Carlisle, S., Chafart, M., and Simonen, K. (2024). The California carbon report: An analysis of the embodied and operational carbon impacts of 30 buildings. Carbon Leadership Forum, University of Washington.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary CLF report/summary checked for 30 new buildings, 60-year scope and 390 kgCO2e/m² median for structure and enclosure.
dataset_overlap_note: Part of CLF WBLCA Benchmark Study v2. Do not add these 30 to the broader 292-project dataset.

study: Benke et al. (2025), dataset and companion CLF benchmark report
setting: US and Canada; real building projects
sample_and_measure: 292 projects; crowd-sourced design-practice LCA models with harmonised inventories and impacts
finding: Open, detailed building-LCA dataset supporting embodied-carbon comparisons and benchmarks
comparison_limit: Two publications from one dataset, counted once; building-LCA scope and possible overlap with other datasets preclude pooling; no governing utilisation
reference: Benke, B., Chafart, M., Shen, Y., Ashtiani, M. Z., Carlisle, S., and Simonen, K. (2025). A harmonized dataset of high-resolution embodied life cycle assessment results for buildings in North America. Scientific Data. Companion: Benke, B., Jensen, A., Chafart, M., Simonen, K., and Lewis, M. (2025). The embodied carbon benchmark report: Embodied carbon budgets and analysis of 292 buildings in the US and Canada. Carbon Leadership Forum.
evidence_access_and_verification: Primary Scientific Data abstract checked for 292 projects and harmonisation. Companion report bibliographic identity checked on the CLF page. Unverified office percentiles are excluded.
dataset_overlap_note: Dataset paper and report describe the same 292-project programme and occupy one entry. Related California/industry inputs must not be added to it.
